content_html:
Free Energy Principle (Bayesian thinking)

The Free Energy Principle (FEP), proposed by Karl Friston, is one of the most ambitious and unifying frameworks in neuroscience. It aims to explain how all living systems - including brains - maintain their order, resist entropy, and adapt to a changing world.

The brain acts to minimize surprise - or more precisely, to minimize variational free energy, which measures the gap between the world it expects and what it actually senses. Every living organism exists in an environment full of uncertainty, yet, despite constant perturbations, it maintains a bounded state - body temperature, chemistry, sensory coherence, etc. To do that, it must:

  • Predict what’s about to happen,
  • Correct errors when predictions fail,
  • Keep sensory states within viable ranges.

Friston’s insight was to express this in mathematical terms - as a minimization of free energy, a quantity borrowed from statistical thermodynamics and information theory. Free energy = a mathematical measure of how well an organism’s internal model of the world matches its sensory input. In Bayesian terms, it’s an upper bound on surprise (the negative log probability of observations given the model). Because organisms can’t directly compute “true” surprise (they don’t know the world’s exact state), they instead minimize free energy, which they can compute. So:

Surprise high → model inaccurate → stress, entropy.
Surprise low → model accurate → stability, survival.

According to FEP, the brain maintains a generative model - a hierarchical probabilistic map that predicts sensory inputs given hidden causes in the world. Each level of the hierarchy predicts the state below it:

  • Higher levels predict patterns (objects, contexts),
  • Lower levels predict raw sensations,
  • Errors (differences) are sent back up to refine predictions.

This recursive structure is called predictive coding - the computational implementation of FEP in the cortex. The free energy principle unifies perception and action under one goal: minimize prediction error.

Process Mechanism What it minimizes
Perception Update internal model to match sensory input Prediction error (via belief updating)
Action Change sensory input to match internal model Prediction error (via movement)

In other words, if your prediction doesn’t fit the world → update the model (perception), or, make the world fit the prediction → act (action). Both serve the same purpose: reduce the mismatch between expectation and experience.

The FEP describes a hierarchical, temporal cascade:

  • Low levels: fast sensory prediction (milliseconds)
  • Mid levels: perceptual categories (seconds)
  • High levels: intentions, self, and identity (minutes to years)

Each level predicts the next, and prediction errors flow upward - forming a dynamic loop that maintains coherence over time. Thus, memory, imagination, and identity are not static stores but ongoing prediction processes across timescales.

The behavioural counterpart of FEP is called Active Inference, which describes how organisms act to fulfil their predictions rather than passively update them. For example:

  • You expect to see your hand in front of you → you move it there.
  • You expect to hear your own speech → you speak.

Action becomes a way of minimizing sensory surprise through movement, guided by expectations. This explains reflexes (fast correction loops), goal-directed behaviour (longer-term prediction fulfilment), homeostasis and allostasis (maintaining internal equilibrium).

Imagine the brain as a scientist inside a dark room:

  • It can’t see the world directly,
  • It only receives a stream of noisy data,
  • It builds a model, predicts what will happen next,
  • When wrong, it revises its model - or changes the experiment (action).

Minimizing surprise keeps its “theories” coherent and its organism alive. Friston generalised this idea to biology itself:

All living systems resist entropy by minimizing the divergence between their internal states and the environment’s structure.

Homeostasis is prediction over physiology.
Learning is prediction over time.
Memory is a compressed generative model of past regularities.
Evolution is prediction at the species level - genes encode expectations about environments that worked before.

Thus, life itself = inference under uncertainty.

While FEP is elegant, critics note:

  • It’s mathematically dense and abstract - sometimes hard to test empirically.
  • It may overgeneralize - describing all adaptive behaviour but predicting few specifics.
  • It’s not clear if brains literally compute free energy, or if it’s a convenient metaphor for optimisation dynamics.

Nevertheless, it unifies many theories (Bayesian brain, predictive coding, reinforcement learning, control theory, thermodynamics) under one mathematical umbrella.

Concept Description Analogue
Free Energy Measure of prediction mismatch “Surprise budget”
Generative Model Brain’s internal model of causes Beliefs / hypotheses
Prediction Error Sensory deviation from expectation Surprise
Active Inference Acting to fulfil predictions Behaviour / control
Precision Weighting Confidence in a signal Attention
Entropy Resistance Maintaining low surprise Life itself

Why it matters for memory and consciousness

  • Memory is the archive of predictive models - used to anticipate future states.
  • Consciousness may arise from the brain’s hierarchical model monitoring its own precision (metacognitive prediction).
  • Dreaming and imagination are simulations that “test” predictions in the absence of real data - offline free-energy minimisation.

Thus, experience, imagination, and behaviour all become facets of one process:

the minimisation of free energy across multiple scales of time.

Bayesian thinking

At its heart, Bayesian thinking is about updating your beliefs when new evidence appears. It’s the mathematics of learning from experience.

  • You start with a belief (a guess about the world).
  • Then you see new evidence (something happens).
  • You combine what you already believed with what you just saw - to form a new belief.

Formally, it’s described by Bayes’ rule:

New belief ∝ Old belief × How well it explains the new data

Situation Prior belief New evidence Updated belief
Weather 30% chance of rain Dark clouds Now ~80%
Medical test 1% of people have disease Test is positive Probability rises - but depends on how reliable the test is
Friend texting Friend usually replies fast No reply for 6 hours Maybe their phone died or they’re busy - belief about cause shifts
Learning in a game “The door on the left is safe” You get shocked opening it Belief quickly drops - you’ll choose differently next time

This is what your brain does automatically: constantly adjusting internal “priors” (expectations) based on “likelihoods” (sensory evidence). The brain is a Bayesian prediction machine: it holds priors (expectations) about what the world should look like, it compares incoming sensory data to those predictions, it updates beliefs to reduce prediction error (surprise).

That’s exactly what the Free Energy Principle describes - it’s a Bayesian brain written in physics language. Imagine your beliefs as a map, and sensory evidence as a compass. The map gives you an idea of where you are (prior). The compass tells you what’s happening now (evidence). You keep adjusting the map so it better fits your surroundings. Over time, the map becomes more accurate - that’s Bayesian learning.

Bayesian reasoning = learning from evidence

Term Meaning Example
Prior What you already believe “It rains 30% of the time.”
Evidence New observation “There are dark clouds.”
Likelihood How well your belief predicts that observation “Clouds are likely if it’s raining.”
Posterior Updated belief after seeing evidence “Now it’s probably going to rain.”

Principles and models

How can matter - which evolved without any explicit knowledge of probability, logic, or models - give rise to systems that seem to embody these principles? The universe doesn’t use models; it is structure. Mathematics, probability, and “Bayesian logic” are not instructions the universe reads - they’re the patterns we can describe after the fact because reality has regularities.

Think of a river carving a valley: the river isn’t computing an energy minimisation, yet its flow obeys the laws that minimise potential energy given gravity and resistance. In the same way, the brain isn’t “solving Bayes’ theorem” explicitly, it’s evolving toward a physical configuration that, by its dynamics, acts as if it were doing inference. Evolution doesn’t need to understand math; it just needs systems that persist - and persistence in a noisy world naturally favours structures that resist surprise.

All matter interacts through energy exchange. When you get self-organising systems (like convection cells, snowflakes, or chemical networks), those structures form because energy flow channels create stable states that balance input and dissipation. Now, add feedback: some of those structures affect the very flows that maintain them. They start to encode information about the environment - not symbolically, but causally. This is the physical seed of representation: a structure whose state carries information about something beyond itself. That’s the first tiny step from physics → proto-inference.

Friston’s deeper claim is that living systems are “self-evidencing.” They maintain their internal organisation by continuously acting in ways that keep them within viable bounds - avoiding disintegration, staying far from thermodynamic equilibrium. Mathematically, that looks identical to a system trying to minimise expected surprise. Life doesn’t know the equations; life is what the equations describe when matter behaves in a self-preserving way. Evolution then selects for those self-organising chemistries that best stabilise themselves - effectively, those that “model” their environment well enough to stay alive.

Emergent coding: from chemistry to neurons

Early molecular systems (RNA, proteins, lipid membranes) already encode regularities:

  • Membrane chemistry “predicts” osmotic pressure gradients.
  • Enzymes “predict” the substrates they evolved to fit.

No conscious model - just structure embodying statistics of the environment. When neurons evolved, they became an explicit implementation of this: synaptic weights encode past regularities, activity patterns predict incoming sensory signals, The organism acts to reduce mismatch. So a nervous system is just matter that has folded back upon itself, creating an internal loop that mirrors the world’s structure.

At a grander scale, evolution itself behaves Bayesianly: each generation encodes prior expectations (genes). The environment provides evidence (selection pressure) upon which successful traits update the gene pool (posterior). The population becomes a distributed learner that refines its implicit model of the world. Natural selection doesn’t calculate probabilities; it enacts them through differential survival. So the mechanics of Bayesian updating can emerge purely from selection under uncertainty.

A brain compresses evolutionary learning into a single lifetime. Instead of waiting for genes to update across generations, neural plasticity lets the organism adjust its internal parameters on the fly - still using the same underlying physics of free energy minimisation. Evolution “discovered” that systems which model their environment efficiently survive better. Brains just made that modelling dynamic, embodied, and fast.

When models become aware of themselves

At higher levels of organisation (conscious brains, societies, science), these implicit physical regularities become explicitly represented: we invent math, probability, and Bayesian reasoning to describe what our nervous systems were already doing unconsciously. So we are the self-reflective instance of the same principle: the universe has produced a structure (mind) that describes its own self-organising tendencies. Mathematics doesn’t precede reality - it’s an emergent mirror of reality’s habit of creating stable, inference-like structures.

Summary

Level Process What “Bayesian” means here
Physics Energy gradients seek equilibrium Systems evolve toward minimal free energy states
Chemistry / Life Autocatalytic networks maintain homeostasis Persistence = implicit prediction of environment
Evolution Selection filters viable structures Population-level Bayesian update
Neural Systems Predictive coding loops Active inference - explicit modelling
Cognition / Culture Language, science, art Meta-models reflecting the same underlying rule

So the universe didn’t start by knowing Bayes’ rule - it evolved systems whose stability behaves according to it. Imagine a coastline formed by waves. Over time, the shoreline’s shape encodes where waves usually break and where rock resists erosion. No plan, no computation - just feedback sculpting form until structure reflects process. The brain is like that: a coastline shaped by the sea of experience, eventually able to describe the ocean that made it.
